title: [2014] Xiaomi Is Becoming the Next Tech Giant, Even If Its Reputation Doesn't Match Its Results
body:
## Top 15 Year in Review: Xiaomi

Regular article

## In 2014, Xiaomi Stopped Being Just a Phone Company

In 2014, the future Xiaomi sketched out went far beyond the "high value-for-money smartphone" it was founded on. According to *The Wall Street Journal*, [Xiaomi closed a new US$1 billion funding round](http://www.wsj.com/articles/chinas-xiaomi-raises-over-1-billion-in-investment-round-1419093589) that values the company at US$45 billion.

How big is US$45 billion? ![Companies with market values near US$45 billion](/uploads/image/201412/6bf60125ff40.jpg)A private company's valuation is not directly comparable to a listed company's market capitalization, but look at the companies worth around US$45 billion: most were founded decades, even a century or more, ago. Airbus, Nissan, Canon... Xiaomi is only 4 years old and has been selling phones for just 3.

In 2013, Xiaomi was still a smartphone maker, mentioned in the same breath as phone brands like Meizu and Lenovo. By the end of 2014, you can no longer talk about China's three tech giants, Tencent, Baidu and Alibaba, without mentioning Xiaomi. The reasons: its fast-growing smartphone business; Mi.com, the country's third-largest e-commerce site; MIUI, a mobile operating system with 85 million users; and the 66 "ecosystem" companies Lei Jun says it has invested in, spanning smart hardware, content and internet services.

## From 200,000 Phones to Number Three in the World

Xiaomi expects to sell more than 60 million smartphones this year. The figure is probably not much inflated: according to the market research firm IDC, Xiaomi overtook Huawei, Lenovo and LG in the third quarter to become the world's third-largest smartphone maker, behind Samsung and Apple.

From 2011 to 2013, Xiaomi phones spread among tech "enthusiasts" who love to tinker, thanks to specs that were good "value for money," "flash sales," and how easy it was to flash custom firmware. According to Xiaomi's own figures, phone sales soared from 215,000 units in 2011 to 18.7 million in 2013.

![Xiaomi's annual phone sales, 2011-2013](/uploads/image/201412/7f63834f2e34.jpg)

Xiaomi also raised this year's target from 40 million units at the start of the year to 60 million, and recently forecast 2015 sales of 100 million phones. That equals Nokia's sales at its 2011 peak.

![Xiaomi's quarterly phone sales in 2014](/uploads/image/201412/067245d7788a.jpg)

Quarterly sales in 2014 (fourth quarter is a forecast)

Xiaomi's fast growth in 2014 came from widening its low-price product line. The Redmi and Redmi Note, mid- to low-end phones priced under 1,000 yuan, reached buyers beyond the "enthusiast" crowd. The Redmi Note, launched in March 2014, passed 10 million sales in just 8 months, faster than either the second-generation Mi 2S or the Mi 3 reached that mark.

![Redmi Note sales compared with the Mi 2S and Mi 3](/uploads/image/201412/e8bd3e536464.jpg)

Over four quarters spanning last year and this, Xiaomi's phone business grew fast enough to catch up with Huawei and Lenovo, the "first tier" of Chinese smartphone makers.

![Major phone makers compared with Xiaomi over the most recent four quarters](/uploads/image/201412/8d885f4e7dcb.jpg) Chart: Major phone makers compared with Xiaomi over the most recent four quarters

After Xiaomi announced a partnership with the Chinese appliance maker Midea in December, the 2013 financials of "Xiaomi Technology" came to light: revenue of 26.583 billion yuan, but net profit of only 347 million yuan, a profit margin of just 1.3%. The revenue figure differs from the 31.6 billion yuan Lei Jun announced at the start of 2014. Xiaomi later said that "Xiaomi Technology" is not the same as the Xiaomi company, but did not say which businesses "Xiaomi Technology" covers or whether it includes smartphones.

## Every Xiaomi Device Is a Gateway

This may be where Xiaomi's innovation lies: "changing the rules of the game at the right moment."

In 2011 it competed on "value for money" and broke down the high price premiums of the smartphone market. It adopted a development model that revises products every week based on user feedback. It controlled its own supply chain by selling through its own e-commerce site instead of relying on distributors. Each year Xiaomi seems to set a new rule for the market. In 2014, every piece of Xiaomi hardware became a gateway.

For traditional phone makers like Nokia and Motorola, the business ends once a phone has been researched, designed, built and sold to consumers through distributors. But in the words of Xiaomi vice president Lin Bin, selling the phone is only the beginning of the business.

Beyond hardware, Xiaomi makes money mainly from its app store and from video content. Games are becoming an important source of revenue for the app store. Xiaomi Interactive Entertainment, the games unit, took in 175 million yuan in November alone, and as of December 14 the Xiaomi game platform's revenue was close to 200 million yuan. According to Xiaomi's official data, its theme store, app store and game center have all become strong content distribution channels: in the first half of 2014, the theme store and app store together recorded more than 35 million downloads a day.

Video is Xiaomi's next content target. Chen Tong, a former Sina vice president who joined Xiaomi in November, has said he will invest a first US$1 billion in content producers. The first deals announced include a content partnership with Youku Tudou and a US$300 million investment in iQiyi.

Video makes its money from advertising. According to iResearch, China's online video market reached 5.43 billion yuan in the second quarter of 2014, up 73.6% year on year, with more than two-thirds coming from ads. More than 80 million Xiaomi smartphones, set-top boxes and TVs will become gateways to video content.

## Smart Hardware, Xiaomi's Moat

Beyond smartphones, what drew the most attention to Xiaomi in 2014 was its push into smart hardware. Lei Jun said in an earlier interview that the "Xiaomi ecosystem" had invested in 66 companies, mainly in smart hardware, software, internet services and content.

Xiaomi usually enters smart hardware by trading "equity for channels" with hardware teams, whose products then join the "Xiaomi ecosystem" program. Once it holds a controlling stake, Xiaomi steps in on product design and pricing, then takes over promotion and sales. Its partners generally fall into two kinds: companies that carry the Xiaomi brand and get a "Mi" name, and hardware teams that keep their own product brand but cut their prices in exchange for Xiaomi's sales channels. Here are some of the hardware companies in the "Xiaomi ecosystem":

![Huami and the Mi Band](/uploads/image/201412/6e686699985c.jpg)

Huami, formerly Zhiqi of Anhui province. Before Xiaomi invested, it developed a range of electronics, such as tablets. After Xiaomi invested this year, it began developing and manufacturing the Mi Band.

![Chuangmi and the Xiaomi smart power strip](/uploads/image/201412/e4b82e38f699.jpg)

Chuangmi is a joint venture between Xiaomi and Longcheer, an ODM that used to make phones for other brands. It now makes Xiaomi's smart power strip.

![The Xiaomi power bank](/uploads/image/201412/770ef261c85a.jpg)

This team's Xiaomi power bank has sold more than 10 million units.

![Zhimi and the Xiaomi air purifier](/uploads/image/201412/bfe949d2a5f6.jpg)

Xiaomi set up this joint venture, Zhimi, only recently. It is run by Su Jun, who leads the Xiaomi air purifier project, and Yuya Omoto, formerly a designer at the Japanese brand Balmuda. The Xiaomi air purifier sells for 899 yuan, but it has been accused of copying Balmuda's AirEngine air purifier.

![The iHealth smart blood pressure monitor](/uploads/image/201412/d11ab12eaa75.jpg)

In the second half of this year, Xiaomi announced an investment in Andon Health's iHealth smart blood pressure monitor. iHealth, originally made for the iPhone, then launched a version for Android phones priced at 199 yuan, much cheaper than the same product in Apple stores.

![Yeelight's color-changing LED bulb](/uploads/image/201412/df6297c3cc9b.jpg)

In October 2014 Xiaomi announced an investment in the Chinese smart lighting maker Yeelight, whose color-changing LED bulb can be controlled from a phone.

![Misfit's health tracking device](/uploads/image/201412/50a20f2651f1.jpg)

In December Xiaomi invested in Misfit, which makes devices that track health data. Misfit's CEO said the company came to Xiaomi precisely for its sales channels.

Why make smart hardware?

It may be the next moat that sets Xiaomi apart from its competitors.

In 2011, while traditional phone makers like Motorola and HTC were still making money from high price premiums, Xiaomi set itself apart with MIUI, its own phone operating system, and with "value for money": a 1,999-yuan phone with specs similar to mid- to high-end smartphones costing 3,000-4,000 yuan. That is why it sold well for 3 years.

In the past two years, phone makers including Huawei and Meizu have adopted the same "value for money" approach and joined the price war. As smartphone prices keep falling and profits grow thinner, Xiaomi has started looking for a future "differentiator" for its brand other than price. Smart hardware is the answer.

Smart power strips, routers and air purifiers can, for now, all be built around Xiaomi phones and software. Like a "moat" around the Xiaomi brand, they make you more likely to choose Xiaomi products because the services and accessories all fit together.

Xiaomi has wavered in this plan, though. In April 2013 it launched the "Mi Router," hoping this high-spec router would become the center of the smart home. The Mi Router has a 1TB hard drive and costs 699 yuan; its main feature is remote-controlled video downloading. Building such a product at a time when licensed video sites dominate, YYeTs has shut down and Xunlei is in decline was clearly a doubtful bet. Xiaomi, which publishes only flattering numbers, now rarely mentions how many Mi Routers it has sold.

In September, Xiaomi dropped its router-centered smart home plan and released Xiaomi Home, a smart home app that looks more dependable: users only need to install it on an iPhone or Android phone to control the smart home products in the Xiaomi ecosystem.

Seeing that smart hardware, and the smart home market in particular, may be the next high ground, phone makers such as Lenovo and Meizu are also trying to enter it, only more slowly and on a smaller scale. Lenovo has its NBD project, which brings in overseas smart hardware teams. Meizu hurriedly started a hardware version of Connect to Meizu in August, selling Chinese smart hardware makers' products in its retail stores. But Xiaomi has already won over a group of the best Chinese smart hardware companies, and that alone is enough to make life hard for any phone maker that wants to copy its invest-and-partner model.

Most of Xiaomi's "smart home" is still just "good-value products you can control with a phone." But like 3D, large screens and high resolution, "smart" and "connected" will become standard features of the next generation of home products, however little people actually use them. Here Xiaomi, by taking equity stakes, has moved faster than any other Chinese company.

## Not Copying Has Become Xiaomi's Biggest Challenge

In past years Xiaomi was criticized for "hunger marketing" and for hiring paid online commenters. In 2014 its biggest problem is copying and patents. After Xiaomi's air purifier was accused in December of copying the design of the Japanese brand Balmuda, a debate over the company's ethics and patents followed. In fact, charges that Xiaomi imitates and copies are nothing new. Here are some of the products that have been cited (images from [Cult of Android](http://www.cultofandroid.com/66569/xiaomi-dont-copy-apple/)):

![Mi 4 and iPhone 5s](/uploads/image/201412/60bb0415b49c.jpg)

Mi 4 and iPhone 5s

As early as 2012, when the Mi 2 came out, some media said its design resembled Meizu's MX2. The 2013 Mi 3 looked like a sibling of the Nokia Lumia. With this year's Mi 4, critics say the model has gone back to the iPhone.

![Mi Router mini and Apple's Magic Trackpad](/uploads/image/201412/9710b6a2233f.jpg)

It is not only phones. Even the Mi Router mini, released in 2014, looks almost exactly like Apple's external trackpad. Other comparisons include:

![Mi Box and Apple TV](/uploads/image/201412/848ad0f23d51.jpg)

Mi Box and Apple TV

![Mi 4 camera promotional image and Apple's Aperture](/uploads/image/201412/864fe415498e.jpg)

Promotional image of the Mi 4's camera features and Apple's Aperture

![Xiaoyi camera and DropCam](/uploads/image/201412/ab33ae7f11bc.jpg)

The Xiaoyi camera and DropCam, which Google acquired this year

![Xiaomi air purifier and Balmuda AirEngine](/uploads/image/201412/2e40d4aa7cf6.jpg)

Xiaomi air purifier (left) and Balmuda's AirEngine air purifier

In October, Apple design chief Jony Ive went so far as to say of Xiaomi in an interview with *Vanity Fair*: "I think it's theft, and it's lazy."

Asked why its smartphones look so different from one generation to the next, Xiaomi vice president Li Wanqiang told QDaily a few months ago that Xiaomi is a young company and has not yet developed its own design language.

But as things stand, the problem will seriously hurt the overseas expansion led by Xiaomi vice president Hugo Barra. At the start of this year, Barra said he wanted results within 2 years. The results Xiaomi delivered this year came mainly from Asian markets with weaker patent protection, including India and Southeast Asia. Not long ago, Xiaomi was hit by a patent dispute in India: Ericsson accused it of infringing its patents, and the Delhi High Court banned sales of Xiaomi phones, which resumed only recently.

After the Balmuda affair and the India ban, Lei Jun said Xiaomi would take 5-10 years to solve its patent problem. As for how, Xiaomi may already have an answer: a Kingsoft company called Zhigu. One of the "Lei Jun family" of companies, its main business is managing intellectual property: developing and licensing high technology and related intellectual property, and business information consulting.

Beyond technology patents, design remains a hurdle Xiaomi cannot get around. The patent war between Apple and Samsung shows that Xiaomi's current products have no chance of being sold normally in Europe or the United States.

Xiaomi is now the world's third-largest phone maker, valued at US$45 billion. How long will it take to develop a design style of its own?

## But Patents and "Copying" Are Not the Core Issue

Perhaps "copying" and patents are only the surface. Xiaomi's real problem in the years ahead is how to become a respected large company worthy of its market position and its fame.

Looking back on Xiaomi's history, from its smartphone designs to how quickly it moved into smart hardware, everything shows that Xiaomi is an extremely good "follower." With its deep understanding of the Chinese market, it can quickly spot what users want, enter a field and do well in it. But that is not enough to become a global company. Xiaomi also needs to compete on technology reserves, corporate brand and a sharp sense of where the industry is heading. Even so, pressing on under the ethical cloud of "copying and imitation" will not necessarily lead Xiaomi to fail.

One counter-example is Jack Ma. In 2011 he moved ownership of Alipay out of Alibaba Group without the board's approval, and both he and Alibaba were accused of breaching business ethics. But because of Alibaba's own commercial success, after its listing the old issues no longer seemed to matter, and few people care to bring them up. Wall Street is a snobbish place, where business ethics always give way to the lure of the market.

For a company like Xiaomi, which could become one of the world's top technology companies, we can still demand more, even if "winners are kings, losers are bandits" is already the common rule of business.

*The Top 15 are: **Apple, [Google](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/4628), Baidu, Alibaba, Tencent, Amazon, [Disney](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/4615), McDonald's, Starbucks, Nike, [Xiaomi](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/4698), IKEA, Uniqlo, Wanda and Vanke.** This list will change as the companies' businesses, markets and trends change. **We will follow them, and their competitors and partners too.*
